description_full: Compass Minerals International, Inc. provides essential minerals in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, and internationally. It operates through two segments, Salt and Plant Nutrition. The Salt segment produces, markets, and sells sodium chloride and magnesium chloride, including rock salt, mechanically and solar evaporated salt, and brine and flake magnesium chloride products; and purchases and sells potassium chloride and calcium chloride to sell as finished products or to blend with sodium chloride to produce specialty products. This segment provides products for use as a deicer for roadways, consumer, and professional use; as an ingredient in chemical production; for water treatment, human, and animal nutrition; and for various other consumer and industrial uses, as well as records management services. The Plant Nutrition segment produces sulfate of potash specialty fertilizers in various grades that are used in broadcast spreaders, direct application, and liquid fertilizer solutions under the Protassium+ brand name; turf products used by the turf and ornamental markets, as well as for blends used on golf course greens; and organic products. This segment provides its products to distributors and retailers of crop inputs, as well as growers. The company was formerly known as Salt Holdings Corporation and changed its name to Compass Minerals International, Inc. in December 2003. Compass Minerals International, Inc. was founded in 1844 and is headquartered in Overland Park, Kansas.

financial_summary: Compass Minerals Intl Inc is a small-cap basic materials business with a $962M market cap on $1.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -0% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.

Returns on capital run at 3% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 23% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.
The business throws off $128M in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
Accruals are elevated at -18.3% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 6.0× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 0.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 23% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
